opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. Coding is the first domain where AI agents are working in a real, economically meaningful way. That's partly because code has a property most domains don't: you can verify it. You can run it, test it, and see if it compiles. That makes it a great environment for reinforcement learning, which is why progress has been so fast.

On the timeline, I'd split it into phases. The first wave was autocomplete, a copilot sitting in your editor finishing your line. That was useful, but it's a fairly thin layer, and it's being commoditized quickly. The wave we're in now is agents that take a task, go off for a while, and come back with a pull request. That's a real shift in how the work gets done, not just a productivity boost.

The next generation of major companies will come from the move to real autonomy. That means systems that understand a large, messy codebase the way a senior engineer on the team does, and that you can trust with meaningful chunks of work without supervising every step. Honestly, the bottleneck there isn't generating code anymore. It's context and reliability: knowing why the code is the way it is, what the organizational knowledge is, and what not to touch. Whoever solves that deeply builds something that looks less like a developer tool and more like a new kind of engineering workforce.

As for when, I think it's sooner than most people intuit. My guess is that over the next couple of years we'll see agents doing a substantial share of the actual engineering work at serious companies. The enduring companies will be the ones that pair frontier model capability with a product that earns trust inside real enterprises. Coding is also a bit of a proving ground. If you can build a superhuman autonomous coder, you've learned a lot about building autonomous systems in general, and that's a big part of why I think it's the right place to focus right now.

r001.rationale: The response cites context and reliability challenges in messy codebases, but does not attribute a longer-than-expected timeline to a gap between enterprise organizational problems and current benchmarks.

r002.rationale: It predicts that substantial engineering work by agents will happen “over the next couple of years,” placing the emergence of the next generation within dozens of months.

r003.rationale: It describes current coding agents, but presents the next generation of major companies as a future result of the move to real autonomy; it does not say those companies are already being built today.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's shorter than most people's intuitions, but longer than the hype cycle wants it to be. If you look at the last platform shift, mobile, the iPhone came out in 2007 and the really durable companies, Uber, Instagram, WhatsApp, got founded in 2009 and 2010. So there's roughly a two to three year lag between the primitive existing and people figuring out what's actually native to it rather than just porting the old thing over.

With coding we're, I'd say, somewhere in the middle of that window right now. The first wave was autocomplete, and that was basically a better version of something that already existed in IDEs. The second wave is agents that can take a task and go run with it for minutes or hours, and that's qualitatively different. That's the thing I'd compare to the iPhone moment, because it changes who gets to build software and how much software gets built, not just how fast an engineer types.

So my guess is the next generation of major companies in this space is being founded right now and over the next eighteen months or so. Some of them will be tools for developers, obviously. But I actually think the more interesting ones are companies where coding agents are the engine and the customer never thinks of it as a coding product at all. It's just that the marginal cost of producing software went toward zero, and some team figured out what you do with that in healthcare or finance or operations.

The caveat I'd add is that the model capability curve is still steep, and that cuts both ways. It means a company founded today might find its core insight gets absorbed into the base model in a year. The ones that make it will be the ones that built around things the model doesn't get for free, which is usually the messy stuff: context about a specific environment, trust, verification, deployment, the long tail of how real organizations actually work. The reasoning will get commoditized. The reliability and the integration won't, at least not as quickly.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a lag between a new platform and native products, and mentions organizational complexity, but it does not attribute the timeline to differences between enterprise problems and current benchmarks.

r002.rationale: It predicts that the next generation will be founded “right now and over the next eighteen months or so,” which is within dozens of months.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says the next generation of major companies “is being founded right now.”

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to separate two timelines. One is: when does AI get good enough to do a large fraction of the coding? The other is: when do companies built around that capability become major companies? Those aren’t the same thing.

You can compress the time it takes to build a product pretty dramatically, but you still have to figure out what people want, get it into their hands, and earn their trust. So I’d expect the next few years to produce a lot of new companies with very small teams that can build things that previously required much larger organizations. It’ll take longer to see which of those become enduring businesses.

The thing I’d watch is how much responsibility you can give the AI. Can it take an ambiguous request, work through the implementation, test it, and determine whether it actually solved the problem? As that gets more reliable, the constraint shifts from writing software toward deciding what’s worth building. That’s where I think a lot of the opportunity will be.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes coding capability from companies becoming major, but does not attribute a longer timeline to enterprise organizational problems versus current benchmarks.

r002.rationale: It predicts many new companies in the next few years, while saying it will take longer to see which become enduring businesses; it does not predict major companies within dozens of months.

r003.rationale: The response forecasts future company formation but does not say the next generation of major AI coding companies is already being built today.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it happens in stages. The first is that existing companies become much more efficient at building software. The next is that small teams can take on problems that previously required hundreds of engineers. That’s where I’d expect a lot of the next major companies to emerge.

The harder question is when AI can own the whole loop: figure out what to build, implement it, see whether people want it, and iterate. Writing code is only one part of that. As code gets cheaper, choosing the right problem and getting feedback from users become more important.

So I’d expect companies built around AI coding to emerge over the next few years. But there’s a difference between when a company starts and when it’s obvious that it’s a major company. We may already be in the first part of that process.

r001.rationale: The response discusses stages and the importance of problem selection and user feedback, but does not attribute a longer-than-expected timeline to a gap between enterprise organizational problems and current benchmarks.

r002.rationale: It predicts that AI-coding companies will emerge “over the next few years,” which communicates a timeline of dozens of months.

r003.rationale: “We may already be in the first part of that process” is tentative and does not clearly assert that the next generation of major AI-coding companies is already being built today.
